claims.text: The undoped Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy undergoes extensive primary crystallization involving several non-eutectic phases.
The undoped alloy exhibits a complex multistep crystallization sequence.
Adding approximately 2 at.% B will suppress nucleation of primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Approximately 2 at.% B will increase retention of the amorphous state.
Approximately 2 at.% B will enhance the alloy's thermal stability.
B incorporation increases local chemical disorder.
B incorporation disrupts short-range ordering that favors crystalline nucleation.
The B-induced structural changes elevate the nucleation barrier for primary crystalline phases.
B impedes the formation of long-range periodic atomic arrangements.
Impeded long-range ordering delays and suppresses the multistep crystallization path during cooling and reheating.
The B-modified alloy will retain a higher amorphous-phase fraction than the undoped alloy.
The B-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature during reheating than the undoped alloy.
The B-modified alloy will show lower-intensity exothermic peaks associated with primary crystallization.
The intervention is expected to be effective at cooling rates above an estimated critical threshold of 10^2 K/s.
The intervention is expected to improve amorphous retention and thermal stability under slower cooling cycles as well as rapid cooling.
Below the estimated cooling-rate boundary, the beneficial effects of B may be diminished.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims enhancement under both rapid and slower cooling, but the boundary states that effectiveness is expected only above an estimated 10^2 K/s critical cooling rate and may diminish outside that range. The slower-cooling regime is not numerically defined or reconciled with this threshold.
